4.Is the court in DiMichel correct in not allowing videotapes to be disclosed until after plaintiff has been deposed? If the court is truly following
a policy of open discovery, why does it matter when the videotapes are disclosed?
5.Less than a year after the Court of Appeals decided the DiMichel case, the New York Legislature enacted Civil Practice Law and Rules

§ 3101(i), which provides, in relevant part:
In addition to any other matter which may be subject to disclosure, there shall be full disclosure of any films, photographs, video tapes or
audio tapes, including transcripts or memoranda thereof, involving a [party; an officer, director, member, agent, or employee of a party; or a
person about to depart the state or for other reasons will not be available; or a person retained as an expert witness]. There shall be disclosure
of all portions of such material, including out-takes, rather than only those portions a party intends to use. * * *
The Court of Appeals subsequently interpreted an aspect of the new law, and held that it had overruled that portion of DiMichel that allowed defendant
to withhold surveillance tapes until after a plaintiff has been deposed. See Tran v. New Rochelle Hospital Medical Center, 99 N.Y.2d 383, 786 N.E.2d
444, 756 N.Y.S.2d 509 (2003). Why do you think the legislature rejected the court’s imposition of a timing requirement on the production of
videotapes?

When defendant files an answer denying the allegations of the complaint, the denials are only that party’s assertions and do not
demonstrate whose story is correct. The motion for summary judgment enables a party to show whether there is admissible evidence to
support the allegations made and to call for a showing by the opposing party. The judge’s role is not to try to decide a factual dispute
when each party has presented competent evidence on an issue and there is a conflict. But if it becomes clear that one party cannot
possibly prove his allegations, there is no “genuine issue” and a futile trial may be avoided by granting the motion.
